newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK term money up,currency down,paper yields mixed.
newsitem.headline: HK term money up,currency down,paper yields mixed.

text.p: Hong Kong interbank term money rates rose on Friday with the local dollar easing further as the market continued to suffer from concerns over Chinese paramount leader Deng Xioaping's health, dealers said.

Three-month money advanced to 5-9/16 17/32 percent from 5-7/16 5/16 at Thursday's close. "People have not yet digested the rumours about Deng Xiaoping. They feel some capital is flowing out of Hong Kong," an Asian bank dealer said.
On Thursday, rumours about problems with Deng's health drove the telegraphic transfer (T.T.) --- the U.S. dollar rate to the Hong Kong unit -- to an intraday high of HK$7.7497 to US$1.00.

On Friday, the T.T. hit an intraday peak of HK$7.7500, the level seen last week when pre-Chinese New Year demand, corporate buying and funds switching out of Hong Kong stocks pushed it to its highest point since January 1995 when it nudged HK$7.77.
The U.S. unit, which is pegged to the local currency at HK$7.8 but has tended to trade between HK$7.73 and HK$7.74 in recent years, stood at HK$7.7493/03 for most of Friday.
"The T.T. is still high. Hong Kong dollar swaps also rose," the trader said.
A weak unit often prompts the government to boost interest rates by selling securities or withdrawing money from banks.
The increase in interbank rates were due also to pre-weekend demand, the dealer added.
Interbank overnight cash rates stood unchanged from Thursday's close at 5 4-7/8 percent, after rising to 5-5/8 1/2 percent at midsession.

One dealer attributed the afternoon fall in overnight rates to a cash injection by the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the territory's de facto central bank, shortly after midsession but this could not be immediately confirmed by HKMA officials.
Exchange Fund paper yields were mixed as overnight falls in U.S. Treasury yields helped to push them down while the weak Hong Kong dollar pulled them up, a European bank dealer said.
Yields of the longest 10-year Exchange Fund notes traded at 6.82 percent on the bid side versus 6.84 at Thursday's close.
Seven-year notes yielded 6.60 percent versus 6.61, the five-year notes yield was unchanged at 6.37 percent and the three-year notes yield was unchanged at 5.95 percent.
One-week Exchange Fund bills yielded 4.70 percent versus 4.67.
